opus-5.5.text:
I think the right way to approach it is to start from the size of the prize. If you take seriously the idea that AI systems could eventually substitute for human labor across a broad range of tasks, not just in narrow domains but in the bulk of cognitive work, you're talking about the share of world output that goes to labor. Globally that's on the order of tens of trillions of dollars a year. Even capturing a modest fraction of that would justify very large investments.

So when people hear "10,000-fold increase in training compute," it sounds wildly extravagant. But a lot of that scale-up comes from hardware getting cheaper per FLOP and from training runs getting longer, not only from spending more dollars. In dollar terms you're plausibly looking at training runs in the tens to hundreds of billions by the end of the decade. That's a lot of money, but it's comparable to what large tech companies already spend on capital expenditure each year. It's not outside what the economy can mobilize if investors believe the returns are there.

The key question is whether investors will keep believing that, and that depends on whether each generation of models produces enough revenue or enough evidence of capability gains to justify the next one. My view is that the case is reasonably strong. We've seen fairly consistent returns to scale, and the revenue from deployed models has been growing rapidly. What you need isn't certainty that you'll automate the whole economy. You need a reasonable probability of very large returns. Even a 10 or 20 percent chance of capturing a meaningful chunk of labor income makes the expected value enormous compared to the cost.

There are real constraints, of course. Power is a big one: building the data centers and grid capacity for gigawatt-scale training is a serious engineering and permitting challenge. Chip manufacturing capacity, particularly advanced packaging and high-bandwidth memory, is another. Data could become a bottleneck, though I think synthetic data and multimodal sources give a fair amount of headroom. When we look at these constraints carefully, none of them seems to rule out that kind of scale-up by 2030, though together they make it harder and more expensive.

So my overall take is that the economic case isn't the weak link. If anything, people tend to underestimate how much value is at stake. The bigger uncertainties are about the physical and logistical constraints, and whether the scaling trends continue to deliver capabilities that translate into real economic value.

r001.rationale: The response argues that large investments in compute could pay off, but it does not say that accelerating labor automation is worth spending a substantial fraction of total economic output.

r002.rationale: It says labor receives tens of trillions of dollars in global output, but does not identify labor as the most expensive factor of production by compensation.

r003.rationale: It puts labor’s share of global output at tens of trillions of dollars annually and says capturing even a modest fraction could justify very large investment, communicating the potential for trillions in annual value.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is you start from what the trend has actually looked like and then ask whether the money and the physical inputs are there to keep it going.

Historically, training compute for frontier models has grown something like four or five times per year. If you extrapolate that out to 2030, you get roughly four orders of magnitude, so about a 10,000-fold increase over what was being used around 2024. And when we went through the inputs, power, chip production, data, latency constraints, our conclusion was that none of those is a hard wall by 2030. They're all difficult, they require enormous buildouts, but they look feasible. So the binding question really becomes: is anyone willing to pay for it?

And the scale of that is important to be clear about. A frontier training run today is on the order of a billion dollars, maybe a few billion if you count the full cluster. A 10,000-fold increase in compute doesn't translate one-to-one into cost because hardware gets cheaper per FLOP, maybe a factor of ten or so over that period, and algorithmic progress makes each FLOP go further. But you're still talking about runs that cost in the hundreds of billions of dollars, and clusters that need gigawatts of power. That's not a line item in an R&D budget. That's a national-scale infrastructure project financed by private capital.

So the economic case has to rest on expected revenue. And here I think the key insight is that the market for AI is not like the market for a normal software product where you saturate some niche. AI is a substitute for labor. The global wage bill is something like fifty or sixty trillion dollars a year. If AI systems can automate even a modest slice of cognitive work, say a few percent of that, you're talking about a trillion dollars or more in annual value. Against that backdrop, spending a few hundred billion on a training run is not obviously irrational. It's more like the kind of bet that a firm makes when it believes it's going after a very large market and that being first matters.

What makes this tricky is that the investment has to be made in advance of the revenue showing up. You're financing capacity in year N based on your expectation of what the model will be able to do in year N plus one or two. So you have this chain: investors need to believe that capability will keep improving with scale, that improved capability translates into products people pay for, and that revenue grows fast enough to justify the next round of investment. Each link in that chain has held so far. AI revenues at the big labs have been growing very quickly, something like doubling or more each year. But the amounts need to keep compounding for several more years, and you need to get to revenues in the hundreds of billions per year to sustain this by the end of the decade.

I'd say there are two ways this could break. One is that the scaling relationship between compute and useful capability flattens out, so you spend ten times more and get something that's only marginally better commercially. The other is that capability improves but the diffusion into the economy is slow, because of integration costs, regulation, organizational inertia, and so the revenue lags the capex by too long for investors to stay patient. Either of those would slow the trend before you reach 10,000x.

But my honest view is that, conditional on the capability trends continuing roughly as they have, the willingness to pay will be there. The hyperscalers already have the cash flows. Sovereign wealth funds and governments are showing up. And the prize, automating a substantial fraction of economically valuable work, is large enough that it's a rational gamble for the actors involved. So I'd put meaningful probability on us actually getting there by 2030, with the main uncertainty being on the technical side rather than the financing side.

r001.rationale: The response calls spending hundreds of billions a rational gamble, but does not argue that accelerating labor automation is worth spending a substantial fraction of total economic output.

r002.rationale: It describes the global wage bill and AI as a substitute for labor, but does not identify labor compensation as the most expensive factor of production.

r003.rationale: It says automating even a few percent of the global wage bill could create “a trillion dollars or more in annual value.”

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between whether a 10,000-fold increase in training compute is technically feasible and whether it makes economic sense. For the economic case, you need to ask how much that compute will cost and what revenues firms can reasonably expect it to generate.

A 10,000-fold increase in compute doesn’t necessarily mean a 10,000-fold increase in expenditure, because the amount of compute you get per dollar should improve. But even allowing for that, you’re talking about very large investments. And the training run is only part of the cost: you also need infrastructure, research and development, and compute to serve the resulting models.

The optimistic case is that these systems become useful across a substantial share of cognitive work. If they can reliably perform economically valuable tasks, rather than just assist with small pieces of them, then the potential market is enormous. That could support investments much larger than those we see today.

But a large potential market isn’t sufficient. Firms need to capture enough of that value as revenue, and ultimately profit, to justify the investment. Competition could drive prices down, adoption could be slower than expected, or capabilities could improve without translating into reliable performance on valuable tasks.

So I’d view this as a conditional case, rather than an inevitable trajectory. Financing that scale of compute becomes much more plausible if successive generations demonstrate both stronger capabilities and growing commercial returns. If those returns disappoint, the economic constraint could bind well before we run out of the technical ability to scale.

r001.rationale: The response discusses conditions that could justify large compute investments, but does not argue that bringing forward AI automation of human labor is worth spending a substantial fraction of economic output.

r002.rationale: It does not identify labor as the most expensive factor of production by compensation.

r003.rationale: It mentions a potentially enormous market, but does not say that capturing a fraction of the value of human labor through automation could yield trillions of dollars per year.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between being able to afford that much compute and having an economic reason to pay for it. A 10,000-fold increase in training compute doesn’t necessarily imply a 10,000-fold increase in spending, because the amount of compute you get per dollar should improve. But you’re still talking about an enormous investment, and the case for that investment depends on what these systems can do.

If AI remains primarily a tool that people pay a modest monthly subscription to use, it’s hard to justify spending on that scale. If it can reliably perform substantial portions of economically valuable work, then the potential market is much larger. You’re looking at spending that could be justified by capturing even a relatively small fraction of the value currently produced by human labor.

The uncertainty is whether additional training compute actually gets you those capabilities, and whether companies can turn those capabilities into revenue. Training a model is also only part of the cost: serving it to customers could require much more compute over its lifetime.

So I’d view this as a conditional economic case. There’s a plausible path where investments of that size make sense, but it requires continued improvements in capabilities and very substantial commercial adoption. And I’d expect the investment to happen in stages, with each generation providing evidence about whether the next, larger investment is worth making.

r001.rationale: The response says large investments could make sense if AI captures some value from human labor, but does not argue that accelerating labor automation is worth spending a substantial fraction of total economic output.

r002.rationale: It refers to value produced by human labor, but does not identify labor compensation as the most expensive factor of production.

r003.rationale: It says capturing a relatively small fraction of labor’s value could justify investment, but does not claim this could yield trillions of dollars per year.
